skill.name: frame-security-scan
skill.description: Scan code (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C#, C/C++) for security vulnerabilities with the open-source Frame CLI or its MCP server, triage the findings, generate and verify fixes, and re-scan. Use when the user asks to security-scan a repo or file, review taint or injection findings, or fix scan results.
skill.summary: Use Frame to scan source code, triage vulnerabilities, review proposed fixes, and verify results with follow-up scans.
skill.author: lambdasec

content.user_title: Scan and Triage Code Vulnerabilities with Frame
content.value_statement: Security scan results need source review before teams can trust findings or apply fixes. This skill guides Frame scans, evidence-based triage, patch review, and verification.
actual_capabilities: Guide Frame scans of files or directories with severity filters, changed-file selection, baselines, and text, JSON, or SARIF output.
Distinguish symbolic findings from LLM findings and report scanner-provided severity, CWE, location, and confidence.
Review source-to-sink flows using a checklist covering attacker control, validation, production reachability, and CWE accuracy.
Request proposed fix diffs through Frame and require consent before applying source changes.
Re-scan patched code, compare earlier findings, and report verification outcomes alongside project test results.
Use connected Frame MCP tools as an alternative to CLI commands, with the same consent requirements.
limitations: Requires a separately installed Frame CLI or a connected Frame MCP server; the skill does not bundle a scanner.
Symbolic scanning covers Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C, C++, and C#; other languages require optional LLM detection.
AI detection and fix generation require an OpenAI-compatible endpoint; hosted endpoints receive code snippets and require consent.
Findings can be missed or incorrect; a clean scan does not establish safety or replace dependency audits.

use_cases.title: Review Application Vulnerabilities
use_cases.description: Scan application code and inspect reported flows before deciding which findings require fixes.

use_cases.title: Triage Security Findings
use_cases.description: Separate symbolic and model findings, inspect validation and reachability, and document evidence for each verdict.

use_cases.title: Check Changed Code
use_cases.description: Use changed-file scans, baselines, and SARIF output to support repository security checks.

prompt_templates.title: Scan One File
prompt_templates.prompt: Check whether Frame is installed, then scan [file] locally without AI. Summarize findings and limitations; do not install software without asking.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: inspect a single source file.

prompt_templates.title: Triage Directory Findings
prompt_templates.prompt: Scan [directory] without AI and save findings. Review each source-to-sink flow and explain confirmed findings, likely false positives, and unresolved questions.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: review a directory with evidence-based triage.

prompt_templates.title: Review and Verify Fixes
prompt_templates.prompt: Triage [findings file], then propose fixes. Ask before endpoint use or source changes; show diffs, re-scan approved patches, and run project tests.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: remediate findings with explicit approval and verification.

prompt_templates.title: Assess Changed Code Against a Baseline
prompt_templates.prompt: Scan files changed since [reference] using [baseline file]. Export SARIF, triage new findings, and explain verification limits without changing configuration.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: evaluate incremental security results for a repository.

output: Scan mode: local symbolic analysis; optional AI was not enabled.
Illustrative finding: a request value reaches a SQL execution sink without parameterization.
Triage: confirmed after reviewing attacker control and the source-to-sink path.
Next step: propose parameterized queries and review the patch before applying it.
A clean scan would not prove the service is secure.

output_examples.input: Illustrative request: compare an approved patch with the earlier scan.
output: Illustrative verification result: the earlier finding is no longer reported after re-scanning.
The reviewed diff replaces SQL string interpolation with parameter binding.
Project tests passed in this example; broader security coverage remains outside the scan.

best_practices: Start with local scanning and obtain consent before sending code to hosted endpoints.
Inspect attacker control, source-to-sink flow, validation, and reachability before assigning a triage verdict.
Review diffs, commit or back up work before approved source changes, then re-scan and run project tests.
anti_patterns: Treating low confidence or a clean scan as proof that code is safe.
Enabling hosted AI or applying source changes without explicit user agreement.
Suppressing findings or trusting model conclusions without reading the affected code.

faq.question: Does this skill install Frame automatically?
faq.answer: No. It checks availability and shows the installation command, but requires agreement before running installation.

faq.question: Which languages support symbolic scanning?
faq.answer: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C, C++, and C# have symbolic frontends. Other languages require optional LLM detection.

faq.question: Does source code leave my machine?
faq.answer: Hosted AI endpoints receive code snippets only after consent. The documented local endpoint supports keeping AI processing on your machine.

faq.question: Can the skill change source files?
faq.answer: It can request proposed fix diffs. In-place source changes require agreement and a commit or backup; fix generation also requires an LLM endpoint.

faq.question: Can I use Frame through MCP?
faq.answer: Yes. A connected Frame MCP server can replace CLI commands, with the same consent rules for AI, source changes, and exploit operations.

faq.question: Does a clean scan guarantee security?
faq.answer: No. Frame can miss vulnerabilities and report false positives. Review findings, verify fixes, and run project tests.
